catalog_citation: Faytak, Matthew & Pius W. Akumbu. 2021 [online 2020]. Kejom (Babanki). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 51(2): 333-354. doi:10.1017/S0025100319000264 (open access PDF, Cambridge Core).
catalog_quote: The most salient prosodic feature of Kejom is its extensive use of tone for lexical and grammatical purposes. At the phonological level, Kejom’s tonal system has been described as a simple opposition between /H/ and /L/ tonemes in various combinations and associations with stem segments (Hyman 1979b). However, a relatively large number of surface tonal sequences are attested; lexical tone of stems is highly ‘mobile’ and spreads progressively to inflectional material; and tone is used for verb inflection ... Tonal contrasts are not evenly distributed in Kejom, with stems exhibiting several contrastive melodies while prefixal material (i.e. noun class inflectional prefixes) is generally only low-toned. Most suffixal material is toneless and receives tone from stems via spreading. ... Kejom contrasts simple high (H) and low (L) tone melodies on monosyllables. In addition, a downstepped hig…

tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. & Valentin Vydrin. 2025. Low tone anticipatory spreading in Babanki: A typological anomaly. Paper presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Societas Linguistica Europaea (SLE 2025), Bordeaux, 26-29 Aug 2025, Workshop 24 'Unifying the comparative analysis of tonal systems' (abstract in SLE 2025 Book of Abstracts, Workshop talks 14-26, p. 1064; HAL halshs-05317130), and at the 34th West African Linguistic Congress, Dakar, 7 Oct 2025 (HAL halshs-05317140).
tone_statements.quote: When nouns come together in such constructions tone behaves in very peculiar ways being constrained by a nasal when it occupies the onset position of noun roots. Hyman (1979) proposes an account of ACs in this language, making heavy use of both floating L and H tones in underlying forms which differ markedly from their surface realizations. He shows what happened historically, retracing the steps that result to the present complex tonal system. ... Monosyllabic noun roots have the structure CV, CGV, CVC, CGVC, NCV, NCGV, NCVC, NCGVC ... with the most common tonal melodies, L and H. ... An essential claim made in this paper is that all prefixes in Kejom are underlyingly low-toned

tone_statements.summary: H vs L tones analysed in Register Tier Theory: raised L, downstepped H, floating L from delinking, falling contour only via docking after schwa deletion; no toneme count stated. At least 50 forms.

tone_statements.quote: Hyman (1979) has demonstrated that Babanki has two underlying tones, namely, High (H) and Low (L), and that on the surface, it contrasts three level tones, H, M, L, plus a downstepped High (↓H). There is also contrast between a falling (L) and a level low (Lo) tone before pause in the language. ... Babanki has two underlying tones, namely H and L, illustrated in (1). ... ndɔ̀ŋ ‘potato’ ndɔ́ŋ ‘cup’ ... It is important to note that contour tones are rare in the language, allowed mainly in a few borrowed words.

tone_statements.summary: Underlying H vs L; surface H, M, L, downstepped H and prepausal level L derived via floating tones and register-feature spread; M and downstepped H equal in F0 (Praat, author's speech); 40+ forms.

tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. & Larry M. Hyman. 2017. Nasals and low tone in Grassfields noun class prefixes. Nordic Journal of African Studies 26(1): 1-13. doi:10.53228/njas.v26i1.94 (open access, njas.fi; author copyhttps://hal.science/hal-03691842v1).
tone_statements.quote: Babanki has four tonal levels. Low (L) and high (H) are basic levels. Before a pause, a falling (LxL) contour is contrastive to the L level tone. M tone results from two processes: – Low tone raising rule (in a sequence of L tones before H, the final L is realized as M), see §6.1.4; – HL simplification rule (the underlying HL on one syllable surfaces as M), see §6.1.2. 3.2. Inventory of tonemes 3.2.1. Tonemes L and H The two tonemes, L and H are shown in the following noun roots which differ only in tone. ... The L toneme has three allotones, level (L), falling (LxL) and rising (LM). ... there is no reason to consider tonal contours as tonemes in Babanki.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemes /H, L/; surface M and downstepped H derived; contours are tone sequences, not tonemes; floating L and H; non-automatic downstep plus downdrift; affix tones fixed or toneless; 90+ forms.

tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. & Larry M. Hyman. 2016. Nasals and Low Tone in Grassfields Noun Class Prefixes. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 12(1): 184-195. doi:10.5070/P7121040730
tone_statements.quote: [p. 188] We know that nasals have a L tone effect on prefixes in WGB (Hombert 1976; Asongwed and Hyman 1976; Hyman 1979b). Asongwed and Hyman (1976: 32) illustrate that prefixal tone is predictable in Ngamambo, a Momo language: CV prefixes have H tone, V prefixes have M tone, and nasal prefixes have L tone. [...] [p. 193] Despite the clear situation in WGB, the literature has not firmly established that nasals (or NC clusters) have a preference for L tone. Drawing on Chichewa data, Trithart (1976) argues that it is possible that NC clusters can have a more important depressor effect on tone than N or C taken separately. Following Trithart, Hombert (1976: 15): suggests “The NC cluster might have had a depressing effect on the fundamental frequency of neighboring vowels which resulted in keeping a L tone on the vowel.”
tone_statements.locator: pp. 188 and 193; Hombert 1976 also cited p. 186 and in the references p. 194

tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. 2011. Tone in Kejom (Babanki) associative construction. Journal of West African Languages 38(1): 69-88. Open author deposit:https://hal.science/hal-03691997v1(PDF file).
tone_statements.quote: Babanki, a Western Grassfields Bantu language of Cameroon, exhibits four surface phonetic levels: H, M, L, and X (a lowered low tone). In the ensuing discussion, it will be argued that there are actually six different tones, or tone reflexes, and that these are derivable from only two underlying tones, given an abstract enough underlying form. ... Since there are no contour tones in Babanki, save for those created by vowel elision, it is unnecessary to adopt a third (language-specific?) WFC.
tone_statements.locator: p. 119, sec. 1 Tonal Alternations; last sentence p. 120, sec. 2 Autosegmental Analysis
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying tones H, L yield surface H, M, L, X; downstep = floating L between anchored Hs; noun melodies e.g. H-HL, H-LH with floating tones; 'TBU' used, unit not named; forms lack tone marks.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 1979. Tonology of the Babanki noun. Studies in African Linguistics 10(2): 159-178.
tone_statements.quote: BABANKI TONAL INVENTORY 4 tonal levels: H, M, L, xL. 2 tonemes: /H/: Floating, Activity, Shared TBU, tonal morpheme criteria. /L/: Floating, Activity, Shared TBU criteria. M is not toneme, it results from surface rules: HL Simplification and L Terracing. xL is not toneme, it appears in the pre-pausal realization of /L/, if not followed by the floating H: kə̀.kòs [L.LxL] ‘slave’ ... Babanki provides evidence of anticipatory low tone spreading that contradicts all known constraints: - The anticipatory L spreading concerns L, not H tone. - The Babanki tonal system is not privative.
tone_statements.locator: slide 6 'Babanki tonal inventory'; after the elision slide 13 'The Babanki anomaly'
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemes /H/ and /L/, four surface levels (H, M, L, xL); M derived by HL simplification and L terracing; floating H posited; three rightward spreading rules and one leftward L spreading (N1 of N2).

sources.citation: Akumbu, Pius W., Larry M. Hyman & Roland Kießling. 2020. The segmental and tonal structure of verb inflection in Babanki. Phonological Data and Analysis 2(2): 1-33. doi:10.3765/pda.v2art2.32 (CC BY, Cambridge Core OA PDF).
sources.quote: 'As seen, verb roots contrast high (H) and low (L) tone, marked with an acute vs. grave accent. Suffixes are underlyingly toneless and take the same tone as the root unless a conflicting suffix tone is assigned by a specific TAM. ... The underlying /H/ and /L/ are subject to various tone rules which produce additional surface contrasts ... there is a third, derived surface-contrastive mid (M) pitch height.' No mention of stress anywhere in 33 pp. (a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits).

sources.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. 2015. Babanki verb tone. Studies in African Linguistics 44(1): 1-26. doi:10.32473/sal.v44i1.107263 (open access, journals.flvc.org).
sources.quote: Abstract: 'An underlying high tone may surface normally as high, but unexpectedly as low, or high-falling; while underlying low tones surface as high, high-falling, or normally as low ... five tone rules (Downstep, Tone Docking, High Tone Spread, Low Tone Spread, and Upstep) and one phonological rule (Schwa Insertion) are required to account for the complex tonal system of Babanki verbs.' Register Tier Theory analysis of /H/ vs /L/; the word 'stress' does not occur (a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits).

tone.quote: Even in Babanki (Central Ring) which has innovated to make all prefixes phonetically low, not all L tone prefixes act alike. As seen in (4a), the majority of L-L nouns become L-M when followed by a H tone. ... The change from root L tone in class 9 to H tone in class 10 as well as downstep of the suffix H are clearly predictable from Proto-WGB. Class 9 was originally marked by a L tone prefix, while class 10 still shows the effects of an original H tone prefix. Synchronically, we can posit corresponding floating tones. ... High tone roots, on their part, cause downstep of suffix H regardless of whether they have a NC cluster or not
